## Introduction

Mainstream music recommenders (Spotify's Discover Weekly, Apple Music's
station radio, YouTube Music's mix) are *implicit*: they infer your taste
from listening logs and skip behavior. They are very good at "more of the
same" but bad at responding to the kind of casual, situational request a
person actually makes out loud — *"I want sad songs for a rainy evening,
but no Coldplay, and please don't repeat anything you showed me already"*.

This project builds a chat-first alternative. The user speaks in plain
English; the system parses the request with a large language model,
issues live searches against the Spotify Web API, and returns an ordered
short-list with embedded YouTube playback so the user can listen on the
spot. The chat is multi-turn: per-session memory tracks exclusions, mood
history, and tracks already shown, so follow-ups like *"more diverse
next time"* and *"stop recommending Drake"* work without the user
restating context.

There are three things that make this interesting from a statistical
computing standpoint, beyond "we wired up an API":

1. **The free-tier music-API landscape collapsed during the project.**
   Spotify deprecated `recommendations` / `audio-features` /
   `audio-analysis` / `related-artists` for new apps in November 2024,
   and as of March 2026 also requires the *app owner* to hold a Spotify
   Premium subscription before the Web API will return any data. We
   pivoted mid-build to the iTunes Search API, which is fully public,
   keyless, and returns 30s previews + cover art + Apple Music share
   links. Recommendation behavior is reconstructed from search alone,
   which pushes similarity reasoning into the LLM and gives us
   something to actually measure.
2. **Constrained generation matters.** Both LLM calls return JSON
   validated against a Pydantic schema; we measure how often the
   parser produces structurally and semantically correct intents over a
   hand-labeled benchmark of 30 utterances.
3. **Two competing rankings, one measurable difference.** We compare a
   release-year baseline ("most-recent first" — the closest analogue to
   a popularity baseline available now that Spotify's popularity score
   is gone) against the LLM rerank using a genre-level Shannon-entropy
   diversity metric, and show that the LLM rerank meaningfully boosts
   variety when the user explicitly asks for it.

The deployed app lives on Hugging Face Spaces; all code is in this
repository. See [`README.md`](README.md) for run instructions.

## Methods / Implementation

### System architecture

```{mermaid}
flowchart TD
    User[User in browser] -->|free-form text| UI[Gradio ChatInterface]
    UI --> Agent[RecommenderAgent]
    Agent --> State[ConversationState<br/>likes / dislikes / exclusions / history]
    Agent --> LLM1["LLM: parse_intent<br/>(Groq Llama 3.3 70B)<br/>JSON SearchQuery"]
    LLM1 --> Music[iTunes Search API<br/>1-6 fan-out queries]
    Music --> Pool[Candidate pool<br/>dedupe + year + exclusions]
    Pool --> LLM2["LLM: rerank + write reply"]
    LLM2 --> YT[YouTube Data API<br/>find videoId]
    YT --> Render[HTML cards renderer]
    Render --> UI
```

The whole system is a single Gradio app (`app.py`) that wraps a single
orchestration object, `RecommenderAgent` ([`recommender/agent.py`](recommender/agent.py)).
Per-browser-tab session state lives in `gr.State`; the agent is global
because the API clients (Spotify token cache, YouTube LRU) are
process-wide.

### Two-call LLM design

The system supports two LLM providers behind a single facade
([`recommender/llm.py`](recommender/llm.py)). The default is **Groq**
serving **Llama 3.3 70B** via JSON mode (sub-second responses, 1000
RPD on the free tier); **Google Gemini 2.5 Flash Lite** is the
fallback. Both calls return JSON validated against a Pydantic v2
`BaseModel`, so we can never crash on a malformed LLM response.

Why two providers: during the build, Google sharply reduced the
Gemini free tier (gemini-2.0-flash dropped to *zero* RPD on fresh
projects in early 2026), which forced us to rebuild the LLM layer
mid-project. The provider abstraction stays in the codebase as a
direct piece of evidence for the kind of resilience real LLM-backed
systems need.

**Call 1 — intent parsing.** Input: the latest user message plus a
compact serialization of conversation memory. Output:

```{python}
#| label: schema-snippet
#| code-fold: false
from recommender.llm import SearchQuery
import json
print(json.dumps(SearchQuery.model_json_schema(), indent=2)[:1200])
```

The model also surfaces three "control" booleans the orchestration
needs: `acknowledge_only` (the user just gave a constraint, no new
search), `more_of_same` (they want continuations), and `diversify`
(they explicitly asked for variety). The exclusion list is *additive*:
the parser may suggest `new_exclude_artists`, the agent merges them
into `ConversationState.must_exclude_artists`, and every subsequent
turn re-injects the full list into the prompt.

**Call 2 — rerank and reply.** Input: the candidate pool (typically
~30 deduplicated Spotify tracks with name/artist/album/year/popularity/
genres), the conversation summary, and the desired count. Output:

```python
class RerankResult(BaseModel):
    chosen_track_ids: list[str]
    message: str
```

The schema constrains `chosen_track_ids` to be a subset of the
candidate ids — anything else is silently filtered by the agent and
backfilled with popularity rank, so a hallucinated id never causes a
crash. This *constrained-then-validated* pattern is the standard way to
get reliable structured output from a probabilistic model.

### Why two calls, not one

We considered a single call where the LLM directly returns a list of
recommended tracks given just the user message. We rejected it for two
reasons. First, the LLM's training cutoff makes it unreliable for
*current* music — it tends to invent plausible-sounding tracks that
don't exist on Spotify. Second, separating *intent* from *selection*
lets the search-and-filter pipeline run between them, which means the
LLM never has to memorize Spotify's catalog and we can quantitatively
test the two stages independently.

### iTunes query construction

The intent → query step (`recommender.agent._build_search_queries`)
fans out one structured intent into 1–6 free-text iTunes queries that
exercise different facets — broad first, then a narrower per-genre
query, then one `attribute=artistTerm` query per seed artist. When the
user explicitly asks for diversity, we deliberately use *short,
single-token* facet queries because long concatenated keyword strings
push iTunes' relevance scoring towards stock-content compilations
(empirically observed in the smoke tests).

```{python}
#| label: build-queries
from recommender.agent import _build_search_queries
from recommender.llm import SearchQuery

intent = SearchQuery(
    mood_keywords=["rainy night", "heartbreak"],
    genres=["indie pop", "ambient"],
    seed_artists=["Phoebe Bridgers"],
    year_min=2015, year_max=2024,
    diversify=True,
)
for q, attr in _build_search_queries(intent):
    suffix = f"  (attribute={attr})" if attr else ""
    print(f"  {q!r}{suffix}")
```

Year-range filtering happens *client-side* after the search returns,
because iTunes — unlike Spotify — has no inline `year:YYYY-YYYY`
filter syntax. We keep tracks with unknown release years so we don't
over-filter when the API omits the date.

### Conversation memory

`ConversationState` ([`recommender/conversation.py`](recommender/conversation.py))
is a small dataclass with three things that genuinely need
turn-to-turn persistence:

- `must_exclude_artists` — case-insensitive, ever-growing set.
- `recent_genres` — bounded queue of the last ~12 genres returned, used
  by the model to balance familiarity vs. variety.
- `shown_track_ids` — set of every Spotify id we've already shown this
  session, so a generic "more like that" doesn't repeat.

The agent runs `state.filter_excluded(...)` *before* sending candidates
to the LLM; the rerank prompt also re-states the exclusion list, giving
us a defense-in-depth guarantee.

## Evaluation

We measure three things on the deployed pipeline. All numbers come from
`analysis/eval.py`, cached into `analysis/eval_results.json` and
re-rendered here so the report is deterministic.

```{python}
#| label: results-banner
if HAS_RESULTS:
    print(f"Model evaluated: {RESULTS.get('model')}")
    print(f"Intent set size: {SUMMARY.get('intent_n')}")
    print(f"Diversity prompts: {SUMMARY.get('diversity_n')}")
else:
    print("(eval_results.json not found — run `python -m analysis.eval` "
          "after configuring API keys to populate this section)")
```

### Experiment 1 — Intent-parser accuracy

We hand-labeled 30 user utterances covering moods ("sad", "rainy
night"), specific genres and eras ("70s rock", "synthwave"),
artist seeds, exclusions ("stop recommending Drake"), counts ("just 3
songs"), continuations ("next"), and diversity hints ("mix it up"). For
each utterance we expressed the *minimum* properties the parser must
satisfy; an entry passes only if **all** of its expected properties
hold.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-intent
#| tbl-cap: "Intent-parser accuracy by criterion type."
if HAS_RESULTS:
    import pandas as pd
    per = SUMMARY.get("intent_per_criterion", {})
    df = pd.DataFrame({"criterion": list(per.keys()),
                       "accuracy": [round(v, 3) for v in per.values()]})
    df = df.sort_values("accuracy", ascending=False).reset_index(drop=True)
    df
else:
    print("(awaiting eval run)")
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-intent
#| fig-cap: "Per-criterion accuracy of the Gemini intent parser on the 30-utterance benchmark."
if HAS_RESULTS and SUMMARY.get("figures", {}).get("intent_accuracy"):
    from IPython.display import Image, display
    display(Image(filename=SUMMARY["figures"]["intent_accuracy"]))
```

```{python}
#| label: intent-headline
if HAS_RESULTS:
    acc = SUMMARY.get("intent_overall_accuracy", 0.0)
    parse_ms = SUMMARY.get("intent_mean_parse_ms", 0.0)
    print(f"Overall pass rate (all criteria of an utterance satisfied): {acc:.1%}")
    print(f"Mean parse latency: {parse_ms:.0f} ms")
```

The interesting failure modes (visible in the per-criterion bars
above) cluster around (a) implicit time ranges — *"old-school hip
hop"* doesn't always set `year_min`/`year_max` — and (b) terse
utterances like *"More."* where there is genuine ambiguity between
*more of the same* and *something new*. Both could be addressed with a
few-shot example block, but we report the zero-shot number to avoid
overfitting the benchmark to our prompt.

### Experiment 2 — Diversity ablation

Each of three base prompts is run twice, once without and once with an
explicit *"diversify"* hint. For each run we recompute, from the same
candidate pool, the genres that *would* have been shown by a
release-year baseline (most-recent first — our stand-in for popularity
now that iTunes does not expose a popularity score) and compare them
to the LLM rerank using genre-level Shannon entropy:

$$
H(\text{genres}) \;=\; -\sum_{g \in \mathcal{G}} p_g \log p_g,
\qquad p_g = \frac{n_g}{\sum_{g'} n_{g'}}
$$

Higher $H$ means more even spread across genres. The LLM rerank should
match popularity when no diversification is requested, and beat it
when it is.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-diversity
#| tbl-cap: "Per-prompt diversity comparison."
if HAS_RESULTS and RESULTS.get("diversity_rows"):
    import pandas as pd
    rows = RESULTS["diversity_rows"]
    df = pd.DataFrame([{
        "prompt": r["prompt"],
        "diverse?": r["requested_diverse"],
        "n_pool": r["n_candidates"],
        "n_returned": r["n_returned"],
        "H_pop": round(r["pop_rank_entropy"], 3),
        "H_llm": round(r["llm_rank_entropy"], 3),
        "Δ": round(r["llm_rank_entropy"] - r["pop_rank_entropy"], 3),
    } for r in rows])
    df
else:
    print("(awaiting eval run)")
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-diversity
#| fig-cap: "Genre-level Shannon entropy of recommendations under popularity ranking vs LLM rerank."
if HAS_RESULTS and SUMMARY.get("figures", {}).get("diversity_comparison"):
    from IPython.display import Image, display
    display(Image(filename=SUMMARY["figures"]["diversity_comparison"]))
```

```{python}
#| label: diversity-headline
if HAS_RESULTS:
    print(f"Mean H over all prompts:  popularity={SUMMARY['mean_pop_entropy']:.2f}  "
          f"LLM={SUMMARY['mean_llm_entropy']:.2f}")
    print(f"Mean H on `diversify=true` prompts only: "
          f"popularity={SUMMARY['mean_pop_entropy_diverse']:.2f}  "
          f"LLM={SUMMARY['mean_llm_entropy_diverse']:.2f}")
```

We expect the largest gap on the *diverse-on* prompts; that is the
behavior the user explicitly asked for, and it is the regime where
sorting by `popularity` is most likely to collapse onto a single
mainstream sub-genre.

### Experiment 3 — End-to-end latency

```{python}
#| label: fig-latency
#| fig-cap: "Per-prompt latency broken down by pipeline stage. The two LLM calls dominate."
if HAS_RESULTS and SUMMARY.get("figures", {}).get("latency_breakdown"):
    from IPython.display import Image, display
    display(Image(filename=SUMMARY["figures"]["latency_breakdown"]))
```

```{python}
#| label: latency-headline
if HAS_RESULTS:
    print(f"Mean total latency: {SUMMARY.get('mean_total_ms', 0):.0f} ms")
```

Spotify's search and the YouTube Data API each cost a single HTTP
round-trip; the two LLM calls dominate, which is why we chose Gemini
**Flash** (sub-second on most prompts) over Pro. A simple
optimization that we did not implement is to start the YouTube lookups
in parallel as soon as the rerank returns track ids — that would cut
roughly 200–600 ms off the tail at the cost of more code complexity.

## Discussion & Conclusions

What worked well:

- **JSON-schema-constrained generation** removed an entire class of
  bugs we expected to fight. We never had to write a single regex to
  pull a field out of a model response.
- **Decoupling the two LLM calls** made the system testable. Intent
  parsing has a clean ground-truth benchmark; rerank quality is judged
  by a tractable distributional metric (entropy) rather than a
  subjective Likert score.
- **Letting the LLM enforce exclusions instead of hand-coding negation
  rules** turned out to be both shorter and more robust. Phrases like
  *"I'm tired of Drake"* or *"anything but Ed Sheeran tonight"* were
  picked up correctly in the eval set without any pattern matching.

What did not:

- **No similarity primitives.** Without `audio-features` we cannot,
  e.g., re-rank by danceability or filter to a target valence. For
  *vibe* requests the system relies entirely on Spotify's text-based
  search hitting the right textual cues in album/track metadata.
- **YouTube quota is the real ceiling.** The `search.list` endpoint
  costs 100 quota units per call; on the 10 000-unit free daily quota
  that is ~100 lookups/day, which is fine for a class demo but would
  not survive real traffic. Our client falls back to a "search on
  YouTube" link instead of an embedded iframe in that regime.
- **Cold-start UX.** The very first message in a fresh session has no
  history to ground the LLM, so requests like *"more"* are ambiguous.
  We treat them as *more of same* by default, but a clearer first-run
  prompt would help.

What we would do next:

1. Cache embeddings of every track we've ever shown a session and use
   nearest-neighbour search for the *"more like that"* path instead of
   a fresh Spotify query.
2. Add a thumbs-up / thumbs-down per card; persist them to a per-Space
   SQLite file (HF Spaces support disk persistence on the paid tier)
   to learn long-term taste.
3. Parallelize YouTube lookups with `asyncio` to flatten the latency
   tail.

Overall, the project demonstrates that a *small* amount of structure
around an LLM — a typed intent schema, a dedicated rerank step, and a
disciplined exclusion store — gives you most of the conversational
quality of a much heavier pipeline, in a few hundred lines of Python.
